note: Language-neutral statements of the R4H-H bounded HTTP/1 host. Each scenario names the exact compiled test that proves it; crates/grapt-api/tests/host_acceptance_corpus.rs refuses a scenario whose owner is not a real test function in the named target. This corpus is H's alone and lives in its own directory: R4H-A owns fixtures/rust-reconstruction/r4-api-auth-foundation under contract grapt-api-auth-acceptance-corpus/v1 and R4H-L owns fixtures/rust-reconstruction/r4-host-auth-foundation under grapt-location-acceptance-corpus/v1, and both validators close their scenario sets in both directions, so a row added to either would turn that lane red. Scenarios whose owner is a `lib` test are there because A's fixture verification route is #[cfg(test)] and unreachable from an integration test; a witness that needs a server-derived principal has nowhere else to live. R1 held this candidate on two defects, both closed here: the root owner's retained task set was unbounded and made the forced-close receipt false, and the architecture gate was red on a fresh default-config checkout. The last four scenarios are their witnesses.

scenarios.claim: A real HTTP/1 request over an accepted location listener reaches the fixture route carrying the server-derived sealed principal, and an explicit stop with nothing in flight returns a graceful receipt whose admitted and refused counts are exact.

A recipient and a client identity authored into a header, a query string and a path never replace the server-derived principal a route sees, and a request presenting no credential does not invoke the route at all.
Exactly the configured number of requests route on one keep-alive connection; the next is a bounded overload refusal carrying Connection: close, and it does not reach the route.
Global request admission answers immediately when the bound is full rather than waiting for a permit, and a released permit admits later work.

An in-flight permit remains consumed after the response head has been produced and is released only when the response body ends or is dropped; while it is held the next request is refused, and releasing the body admits one.
Live admitted sockets never exceed the connection bound: an additional client is not admitted into a connection task while the bound is full, and is served once a permit returns.

A connection permit is released when its task ends, not when its response was written: while the first connection is still live the terminal receipt reports exactly one admitted connection, however many clients connected.
A consuming route observes no more than the configured body bytes and answers 413; a known oversized Content-Length is refused ahead of the route without invoking it at all.
A stop issued while a response body is still open keeps polling that connection after signalling graceful shutdown, and a body that completes before the drain deadline yields a graceful receipt.
An exhausted drain allowance snapshots the exact live connection count, aborts and joins every one of them, and returns a forced-close receipt that is never rendered as graceful.
One classified accept failure fails the host typed at the accept stage after exactly one attempt, with no retry schedule and no inspection of operating-system text.
Every accept failure is classified from an io::ErrorKind or from the listener's own closed refusal, including kinds a witness cannot make a real socket produce.
A root task that ends without producing a receipt is reported as that loss, naming whether it was detached, cancelled or panicked, rather than as a fabricated live-resource count nobody measured.
All eight host bounds refuse zero and each refusal names its own field rather than a sibling's.

A head buffer below the HTTP/1 backend's minimum is refused typed, reporting both the supplied value and the backend's minimum, without reaching the assertion that would panic; the minimum itself is admitted.
Both semaphore-backed bounds refuse a count above the permit backend's maximum before the semaphore is constructed, and the maximum itself is admitted.
A counter increment past the u64 ceiling is reported as an overflow that fails the receipt typed, and the counter holds its last true value rather than wrapping.
All four timing methods the HTTP/1 connection uses route to the injected driver, including the reading of now whose trait default is an ambient wall clock.
The production driver's reading of now moves with the runtime clock, so a witness can advance a deadline instead of waiting for one.
A head carrying more headers than the bound is refused by the parser with 431 before the authenticated service, while a well-formed request on the same host reaches the service and is refused there.
A head larger than the configured read buffer never reaches the authenticated service, under a header-count bound set high enough that it cannot be the bound in force.
Under deterministic time an incomplete head is closed without any response once its allowance is exhausted, while a complete head on the same paused clock is answered without touching the deadline.
An unauthenticated request declaring an oversized body is refused before its body is considered at all, so the host reads none of it and tells the caller nothing about its bounds.
A host proven to be serving is stopped while its accept is pending; the stop cancels that accept, the root joins, and the address serves nothing afterwards.
The host consumes the listener by value and gives the socket up at its terminal: the exact observed address can be rebound by a new location owner once the host has joined.
Dropping a running host stops it serving and returns no receipt, because durable finalization that needs input or output may not be assumed to complete inside Drop.

No production module contains the convenience server, the automatic protocol builder, an upgrade, HTTP/2, an unbounded channel, an ambient clock reading, an unwrap, an expect, unsafe code, or a lint suppression.
The connection task is spawned in exactly one place and that spawn moves the already-acquired connection permit into the task.
No production module outside the named deadline adapter reaches a clock, and the adapter itself does, so the placement check is about placement rather than about absence.
The compiler rejects a defaulted limit set, a listener used after transfer into the host, a cloned running host, and a raw router passed where the sealed authenticated service is required.

The root owner reaps completed connection tasks unconditionally, so its retained task set never exceeds max_connections however many sequential connections have been served, and every connection is still counted exactly once.
A terminal receipt never reports more connections live at the deadline, or aborted and joined, than the connection bound admits could ever have been live at once.
Under the production driver and a genuinely exhausted drain allowance, a run in which every response completed reports no forced-close backlog it did not have.

The architecture gate's test-module stripper cuts identically on an LF and a CRLF checkout, so a crate's legitimate test-only clock use is never scanned as production source because of how the tree was checked out.
